GM Canada's Oshawa Assembly Plant Hits 600,000th Chevrolet Silverado Production Milestone
17 photos
Photo: GM Canada
600,000 trucks in five years isn't a bad result for a factory that was previously found itself on the brink. The Oshawa complex resumed truck production in November 2021, and the Ontario-based facility is celebrating another milestone as it prepares for nearly CAD 500 million in additional investment for the next-generation Chevrolet Silverado HD and GMC Sierra HD.
More than 600,000 trucks in the span of 60 months is a tremendous result, working out to 120,000 vehicles annually. GM's Canadian subsidiary hasn't provided a year-by-year production breakdown, yet the cumulative figure shows how quickly a once-doomed plant can re-establish itself authoritatively.
Said 180-degree turn was not guaranteed, though, albeit North America has a big appetite for large trucks. Back in November 2018, the Detroit-based automaker made it clear that Oshawa would end vehicle production by December 2019. Instead, the company would have converted Oshawa to stamping, subassembly, and less important manufacturing activities.
No fewer than CAD 170 million supported the downgrade, yet a reversal came in November 2020. The Big G announced that full-size truck production is the name of the game, retooling the facility and recruiting workers as it prepared for a two-shift operation. The reopened assembly line started churning out Silverados on November 10, 2021, creating 1,800 new jobs at the plant while supporting thousands more throughout Canada's automotive supply chain.
The Silverado program is the latest chapter of a story that started in November 1953. Over the years, Oshawa has built everything from lousy Pontiacs and Buicks to the Chevrolet Camaro. During WWII, tanks and machine guns were the norm. The Cadillac XTS and Chevrolet Equinox were assembled there as well. Before the 2019 shutdown, it specialized in Silverado and Sierra pickups.
Photo: GM Oshawa accommodates both light- and heavy-duty truck production alongside stamping, subassembly, and aftermarket parts production. Regarding the latter, June 2026 saw the plant pass 1 million aftermarket parts produced since the 2021 restart. Come December 2026, the Canadian facility will make the switch to the 2027 model year Chevrolet Silverado HD, new diesel engine and all.
The L6P turbo diesel, which is the largest one yet at 8.3 liters, comes from the DMAX plant in Brookville, Ohio. As for the lesser L8S gasoline V8, that one is assembled at Tonawanda Propulsion in Buffalo, New York. While both mills are neat in their own ways, the Duramax is the one to have for effortless towing.
Beyond the revised engine lineup, the 2027 model year Silverado HD further prides itself on new trailering, braking, and steering technologies. Going forward, those CAD 500 million will be invested over the next three years. The investment can be split between 343 million for truck production and various additional improvements, and 144 million to bring the next-generation Sierra HD.
The investment in question is connected to St. Catharines Propulsion, where more than CAD 900 million has been committed for V8 and transmission production. Said programs support the full-size truck and SUV lineup across North America, meaning that engines and transmissions from St. Catharines Propulsion will eventually be used by the Tahoe, Suburban, Yukon, and Escalade.
Five years ago, the question was whether Oshawa would build vehicles again. Today, making preparations for another generation of trucks is a win for both the largest automaker of the Detroit Big Three and the approximately 3,100 workers operating there on a two-shift schedule.
